questions.prompt: The gradient of \(c^{T} x\), with \(c\) constant, is
options: the matrix with \(c\) on the diagonal
questions.explanation: Each coordinate derivative of a linear form is the matching entry of \(c\), so the gradient is \(c\). The scalar \(c^{T} x\) is the function value. The gradient is zero only when \(c\) is zero. A diagonal matrix would be a Hessian-sized object; the Hessian of a linear form is the zero matrix.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(f(x) = x^{T} A x\). At \(x = (1, 1)\), what is the first entry of \(\nabla f\)?
questions.explanation: Expanding gives \(x_1^2 + 3 x_1 x_2 + 2 x_2^2\). The partial derivative in \(x_1\) is \(2 x_1 + 3 x_2\), which equals 5 at \((1, 1)\). The formula \((A + A^{T}) x\) gives the same vector \((5, 7)\). Using \(2 A x\) instead, as if \(A\) were symmetric, gives \((8, 4)\), and the first entry of that vector is 8.

questions.prompt: For a square \(A\) that is not assumed symmetric, \(\nabla (x^{T} A x)\) equals
questions.explanation: Differentiating the sum \(\sum_{ij} a_{ij} x_i x_j\) hits each factor once, which produces \(A x\) from one order and \(A^{T} x\) from the other. The factor \(2 A x\) is the special case \(A = A^{T}\). Using \(A x\) alone drops the transpose term. The product \(A^{T} A\) appears in a squared residual, not in \(x^{T} A x\).

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 array with four letter entries.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}\). The partial derivative of \(x^{T} A x\) with respect to the first coordinate is an expression in the names p, q, r, x, and y, where \(x\) and \(y\) are the two coordinates. Write that expression.
questions.explanation:
The quadratic is \(p x^2 + (q + r) x y + s y^2\). Differentiating in \(x\) gives \(2 p x + (q + r) y\). The diagonal entry \(s\) multiplies \(y^2\) only, so it does not appear in this partial derivative.
• \(2 p x + q y\) keeps only one of the two off-diagonal contributions.
• \(2 p x + 2 q y\) is the symmetric formula, and it is wrong when \(r\) is not equal to \(q\).
• \(p x + (q + r) y\) misses the 2 on the square.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(f(x) = x^{T} A x\). At \(x = (1, 1)\), what is the second entry of \(\nabla f\)?
questions.explanation: The partial derivative in the second coordinate is \(3 x_1 + 4 x_2\), which equals 7. It is the second entry of \((A + A^{T}) x\). The first entry is 5. The second entry of \(2 A x\) is 4, which is the symmetric-formula mistake. The function value is \(1 + 3 + 2 = 6\), not a partial derivative.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(b = (1, 0)\), and \(x = (2, 1)\). For \(f(x) = \lVert A x - b \rVert^2\), what is the first entry of \(\nabla f\)?
questions.explanation: \(A x - b = (1, 5)\). Then \(A^{T}(A x - b) = (11, 5)\), and the gradient is twice that vector, so the first entry is 22. The residual sum of squares is \(1 + 25 = 26\), which is the function value. The second entry of the gradient is 10. Using \(A\) instead of \(A^{T}\) on the residual produces \((1, 7)\), and twice the first entry of that vector is 2.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to differentiate \(x^{T} A x\) in coordinates.
questions.explanation: The sum is the object being differentiated, so it comes first. Differentiation in one coordinate is next. The product rule splits into two groups, and only then can those groups be recognized as \(A x\) and \(A^{T} x\). Starting from \(2 A x\) skips the split and is valid only after \(A\) has been replaced by its symmetric part.

steps: Write the form as a sum of a_ij x_i x_j over both indices.
Differentiate that sum with respect to one coordinate x_k.
Separate the hits on the left factor from the hits on the right factor.
Read the two groups as the matching entries of A x and of A transpose x.

questions.prompt: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), the Hessian of \(x^{T} A x\) is \(A + A^{T}\). What is the \((1, 2)\) entry of that Hessian?
questions.explanation: \(A + A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), so the off-diagonal entry is \(3 + 0 = 3\). Twice the off-diagonal entry of \(A\) is 6, which would be right only if the other off-diagonal entry were also 3. The \((2, 2)\) entry of the Hessian is 4. The \((1, 1)\) entry is 2.

questions.explanation: The squared Euclidean length is \(x^{T} x\), and the symmetric-formula gives \(2x\). The vector \(x\) misses the factor 2. The length \(\lVert x \rVert\) is a different function, whose gradient is the unit vector where \(x \ne 0\). The outer product \(x x^{T}\) is a matrix, not the gradient.

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
questions.explanation: The matrix really is nonsymmetric, and \(2 A (1, 1) = 2(5, 3) = (10, 6)\), so the last step only evaluates the formula above it. The false step is the formula. The gradient is \((A + A^{T}) x\). Here \(A + A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\), and the product with \((1, 1)\) is \((6, 10)\).

steps: Let f(x) = x transpose A x.
A is not symmetric, because its off-diagonal entries are 4 and 0.
The gradient of x transpose A x is 2 A x for every real square A.
At x = (1, 1), that formula produces the vector (10, 6).
reasons: The gradient is (A + A transpose) x. The formula 2 A x needs A to be symmetric.
The matrix is symmetric, so the comparison of off-diagonal entries is the false step.
The gradient is A x, with no factor 2 and no transpose.

questions.prompt: At \(x = (3, 4)\), what is the first entry of the gradient of \(\lVert x \rVert^2\)?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \(2x\), so the first entry is \(2 \cdot 3 = 6\). The coordinate 3 itself misses the factor 2. The second entry is 8. The function value is \(9 + 16 = 25\). Half of 6 is the coordinate, not the partial derivative.

questions.prompt: A quadratic \(f(x) = \tfrac12 x^{T} A x + b^{T} x\) with symmetric \(A\) has gradient
options: \(x^{T} A + b^{T}\), kept as a row
questions.explanation: The factor one half cancels the 2 from differentiating \(x^{T} A x\) when \(A\) is symmetric, and the linear term contributes \(b\). Leaving the one half in front of \(A x\) double-counts the cancellation. A row is the Jacobian layout, not the column gradient used here. Adding the matrix \(A\) to the vector \(b\) is not a defined gradient.
